23138-diary-in-america-series-two:
Procrastination opens Diary in America, series two. Knowing a sight can be seen any time, the diarist reflects, people delay until they never see it at all. He recalls a lifelong Londoner who meant every year, for decades, to visit the Tower at last.

Frederick Marryat's second series continues his American tour, prisons, schools, and frontier settlements among its stops. The Tower joke does quiet work, a traveler's confession that familiarity blinds natives and visitors alike. Marryat writes as a naval officer abroad, direct about what he admires and what he finds absurd. Paired with the first series, the diary gives a full, opinionated portrait of Jacksonian America from a British deck, so to speak, still rolling under his sentences.

nasa-tm-19670030822-standard-payload-mod:
Preston T. Farish, of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, wrote this planning memorandum on July 22, 1965. It presents a standard definition network for payload module work, covering project Phases A through D. A definition network maps the tasks and decisions that turn an idea into approved hardware.

Farish offers the information as a guideline for managers. Its aim is the soundest practical management baseline for planning, approval, and execution of future programs. The standard payload module is the example throughout. The abstract promises the network and concept proposal, with early definition material, as the core of the document.
podcast-joerogan-9-z0kglwpwo:
Gerontologist Aubrey de Grey joins Joe Rogan for episode 1432 of the Joe Rogan Experience. De Grey is a top voice for the claim that aging is a disease that can be cured. His work aims to fix the harm that builds in cells with age.

De Grey lays out the seven kinds of cell harm he says drive old age and death. He argues each can be fixed with care that is near at hand. Rogan asks when a normal man might see such care. Listeners get the boldest case in the youth field. The library keeps the episode as a record of his stated work.
podcast-tuckercarlson-YGRMp-GkIwo:
Strategist Steve Bannon talks with Tucker Carlson after a court orders him to prison. Bannon had refused a subpoena from the January 6 panel. He presents the sentence as political punishment.

He stays defiant in tone from the first minute. The title calls his reply the subject, and nothing else crowds it. Bannon vows that prison will not silence his movement work. Carlson treats him as a prisoner of conscience. The episode preserves a key ally's last public stand before serving time, aimed at loyal fans. His base hears a call to keep fighting.
poems-by-emily-dickinson-series-two:
Emily Dickinson's second series of Poems followed the success of the first posthumous volume, bringing more of her manuscripts into print. Dickinson had spent her life in Amherst, Massachusetts, writing lyrics of extraordinary compression and keeping them in hand-sewn packets at home. The first series proved that readers existed for this strange, private work; a second helping followed at once.

Like its predecessor, the volume draws on the store of poems she left behind, treating the same great subjects. Death and immortality, the natural world watched from a garden, love, pain, and the life of the mind. Her habits are all here, the dashes, the capital letters mid-line, the hymns that swerve into doubt. Together the early series built the reading public that made Dickinson a central American poet.
poems-teachers-ask-for-book-two:
Teachers chose the contents of this anthology themselves. Poems Teachers Ask For, Book Two, gathers more than two hundred poems that readers of the magazine Normal Instructor-Primary Plans had requested for its page of poems readers asked for. The result is a working schoolroom library: the pieces American teachers actually reached for when they needed a poem for a holiday. A memorial, a recitation, or a rainy Friday afternoon.

The index reads like a roll of the era's school canon: Poe's Annabel Lee, Kipling's Ballad of East and West. Tennyson's Break, Break, Break, Whittier's Barbara Frietchie in the companion tradition, and patriotic set pieces for flag days. Sentimental, moral, and seasonal poems fill the rest, each with a classroom use. Books like this one, chosen from below by working teachers, show what poetry meant in ordinary American schools before the anthology trade professionalized the canon.
songs-of-two:
Arthur Sherburne Hardy dates Songs of Two to 1900, and the poems speak in a lover's voice of parting and faith. The first poem dreams that the singer is dead and hears a footstep on the sod above. The Dear one touches his breast and asks what she shall write against his name for men to see. Quick comes the answer: I was beloved of thee.

The second poem looks down a path that splits, where the two must walk alone a little space. The singer vows to wait strong with memory alone till he sees her face. Yet he turns, in sore need, to beg her giving grace once more. At the last parting, when night hides her smile, his hand shall seek her own and hold it fast.
the-dead-boxer-the-works-of-william-carl:
William Carleton's The Dead Boxer opens one evening near the end of April in the beginning of the eighteenth century, about the year 1720 by the narrator's guess. A young man named Lamh Laudher O'Rorke, or Strong-handed O'Rorke, walks with a stout oaken cudgel. He heads toward an orchard at the skirt of a country town in a part of Ireland left nameless.

His Christian name is John, Carleton explains. Irish families of one name were told apart by nicknames drawn from build, speed, or look: swift Paddy, yellow Jack, big Michael, red James. John and his forefathers earned theirs through great bodily strength and courage. The pale sun hangs over western hills as he saunters, slow with quiet delight in the opening summer. He meets a stout, muscular older woman in a red woollen petticoat and blue hose, carrying a short oaken staff.
